# stream-sorting — full reference

External merge sort and sorted-stream operations for object-mode Node `Readable` streams. Part of the `stream-chain` / `stream-json` / `stream-join` family. This file is the long-form AI-facing reference; `llms.txt` is the short summary.

## Status

All operations are implemented (the package has not yet published its first npm release): the wrapper protocol, two built-in wrappers (`MemoryWrapper`, `LocalFileWrapper`), both sort algorithms (`sort`, `polyphaseSort`), the join family (`join`, `leftJoin`, `fullJoin`), `aggregate`, the key-based filters (`matching`, `unmatched`), and the set operations (`merge`, `union`, `intersection`, `difference`). Remaining work is tracked in `projects/stream-sorting/queue.md` in Eugene's vault.

## Object-stream wrapper protocol (shipped)

The wrapper protocol — base classes, helper, and contract docs — lives at `src/wrapper.js`. Every algorithm in the package operates against `ObjectStreamWrapper<T>`. The contract is **runtime-agnostic** — no `node:stream` or Web Streams types appear — so each wrapper picks its own internal mechanism (Node FS streams, AWS SDK, async generators, Web Streams, etc.) without changing the algorithm:

```ts
class ItemWriter<T = unknown> {
  // Backpressure-aware: resolves when the item has been accepted by storage.
  write(item: T): Promise<void>;                                  // abstract
  // Drain an iterable; awaits each write so the source pulls at the writer's pace.
  // Does NOT call end() — compose the two explicitly, or use consume().
  // Base implementation: serialized loop that calls write(item); override only if
  // the storage offers a smarter bulk path (e.g., a single backend call).
  writeAll(source: AsyncIterable<T> | Iterable<T>): Promise<void>;
  // MUST be idempotent: second and later calls return the same promise as the first.
  end(): Promise<void>;                                            // abstract
  // MUST flip to true synchronously inside the first end() call.
  readonly ended: boolean;                                         // abstract
}

class ObjectStreamWrapper<T = unknown> {
  openWriter(): ItemWriter<T>;
  openReader(): AsyncIterable<T>;
  close(): Promise<void>;   // coarse-grained: abandon current mode
  delete(): Promise<void>;  // idempotent; removes underlying storage
}
```

Both are real JS classes. `extends ItemWriter` gives subclasses the default `writeAll` loop (and `instanceof` works for runtime checks); `extends ObjectStreamWrapper` is a marker that documents intent. Plain objects matching the shape also satisfy the contract — TypeScript accepts either, JavaScript runs either.

**Mode-exclusive.** A wrapper is `idle`, `writing`, or `reading` at any moment. `openWriter()` while writing re-opens and discards previous content. `openReader()` while writing throws — call `close()` first. `openWriter()` while reading throws. Both built-in algorithms (`sort`, `polyphaseSort`) write-then-read; they never use both modes concurrently. Custom wrappers MUST honor these rules.

**Cleanup via `return()`.** The iterator returned from `openReader()[Symbol.asyncIterator]()` implements `return()`. `for await ... break`, thrown exceptions in the loop body, and explicit `iterator.return()` all release per-read resources automatically — no manual close needed. `wrapper.close()` is the coarse-grained escape hatch for sessions abandoned without iterating, or as defensive cleanup before `delete()`.

**`consume(writer, source)` helper.** Lives in `src/wrapper.js` alongside the bases. One-shot convenience equivalent to `await writer.writeAll(source); await writer.end();`. Use when you have all items in hand:

```js
import {MemoryWrapper, consume} from 'stream-sorting';

const m = new MemoryWrapper();
await consume(m.openWriter(), [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]);
for await (const item of m.openReader()) console.log(item);
```

**Built-in wrappers (shipped, zero extra deps):**

```js
import {MemoryWrapper, LocalFileWrapper} from 'stream-sorting';

// In-memory; for tests, small data, benchmarking the algorithm without disk.
const m = new MemoryWrapper();

// Local filesystem; JSON-line-delimited by default.
const f = new LocalFileWrapper({path: '/var/sort/run-0.jsonl'});

// Custom per-item encoding (still line-delimited; result must not contain '\n').
const fBin = new LocalFileWrapper({
  path: '/var/sort/run-0.dat',
  serialize: item => myEncode(item),
  deserialize: text => myDecode(text)
});

// Imperative writer:
const w = f.openWriter();
await w.write({id: 1});
await w.writeAll([{id: 2}, {id: 3}]);
await w.end();
```

`LocalFileWrapper`'s `path` is required: there is no default `tmpDir`, because Linux `/tmp` is commonly tmpfs (RAM-backed) and would silently defeat the disk-backed sort. The wrapper exposes its path via the read-only `wrapper.path` getter. Default framing is `JSON.stringify(item) + '\n'` per line; on read, stream-chain's `gen(fixUtf8Stream(), lines(), deserialize)` pipeline handles UTF-8 reassembly across chunk boundaries and tolerates either trailing-newline or no-trailing-newline files. The framing is compatible with `stream-chain`'s `jsonl/parserStream`.

Custom wrappers for S3, SSH-pipe, sharded volumes, etc., satisfy the interface structurally — see `dev-docs/initial.md` § "Object-stream wrapper protocol" for recipes.

## Design context

### Why a separate package

The `stream-*` family separates concerns by *what the operation knows about the data*:

- **`stream-chain`** — pipeline plumbing. Knows nothing about data shape.
- **`stream-json`** — JSON streaming. Knows about JSON tokens.
- **`stream-join`** — N→1 combinators. Knows about Readable streams but **not** about sortedness or keys.
- **`stream-fork`** — 1→N split / route / filter. Knows about predicates but not sortedness.
- **`stream-sorting`** — **knows about sortedness**. Anything that requires sorted input or produces sorted output lives here.

The split was settled 2026-05-18 during the stream-join 2.x scope-rationalization pass. `stream-join` deliberately rejected being a home for sort and sort-dependent ops; this package picks them up.

### Why Node-only

Sorting at billion-record scale is fundamentally a server / CLI problem. The headline `sort` is disk-backed via `node:fs`, `node:os`, `node:path`; there is no sensible browser equivalent of "spill sorted runs to local storage." The package has no web entry point and no browser test surface, and we don't plan to add either.

### Why disk-backed external merge sort

Three strategies were considered for the sort engine:

1. **In-memory full buffer** — pulls the entire input into an array, sorts, emits. Simple, but scales to RAM only. Rejected for the package's design point.
2. **Sliding-window approximate sort** — buffer the last N items, emit min on every advance. Constant memory, but does **not** actually sort if the input's disorder exceeds the window. Rejected as a misleading API.
3. **Disk-backed external merge sort** — pull into a memory-bounded buffer, sort + flush to disk as a run, repeat until input ends; k-way-merge the runs streaming-style. Sorts at arbitrary cardinality regardless of memory. **Chosen.**

The design point is "sort a billion records on a laptop without OOMing." In-memory sort isn't an API surface this package needs because `await stream.toArray()` + `Array.prototype.sort(compare)` is already one line of user code; the value-add is the part that doesn't fit in memory.

### Why depend on `stream-join`

The k-way-merge phase is exactly the shape `stream-join`'s `select(streams, options)` was designed for, with `sortedInsert(lessFn)` as the `insert` callback and `pickFirst` as the `pick` callback. Reusing those primitives instead of reimplementing is intentional — it keeps the merge logic in one place, tested in one place, and the two packages co-evolve naturally.

Both `stream-chain` (`^4.0.2`) and `stream-join` (`^2.0.0`) are declared in `dependencies`; component implementations compose their primitives directly.

## Module system

ESM only (`"type": "module"`). Source files use `import` / `export`; tests likewise. Subpath imports must include the `.js` extension because the `exports` map wildcards `"./*": "./src/*"`:

```js
import sort from 'stream-sorting/sort.js';            // → ./src/sort.js
import {LocalFileWrapper} from 'stream-sorting';      // → ./src/index.js
```

## API reference

### `sort(input, options)` — external merge sort (shipped)

Sorts an iterable of any cardinality. `input` is `AsyncIterable<T> | Iterable<T>` (Node Readables, Web ReadableStreams, generators, and arrays all satisfy). Returns an `AsyncIterable<T>` (an async generator) — user converts at the boundary to whatever stream type they want, paying the per-runtime cost only where they need it.

**Signature:**

```ts
function sort<T>(
  input: AsyncIterable<T> | Iterable<T>,
  options:
    | {compare: (a: T, b: T) => number}
    | {lessFn: (a: T, b: T) => boolean}
    & ({tmpDir: string} | {createWrapper: (runIndex: number) => ObjectStreamWrapper<unknown>})
    & {
        batchSize?: number;       // default 10000
        stable?: boolean;          // default true
        onProgress?: (stats: SortProgressStats) => void;
        keepTempFiles?: boolean;   // default false
      }
): AsyncGenerator<T, void, void>;
```

**Parameters:**

- `compare` OR `lessFn` (exactly one required) — comparator. `compare(a, b)` returns negative if `a < b`, positive if `a > b`, zero if equal (`Array.prototype.sort` style). `lessFn(a, b)` returns `true` if `a` should come before `b` (matches stream-join's primitive). Internally normalized to whichever the consuming step needs.
- `tmpDir` OR `createWrapper` (exactly one required) — storage strategy. `tmpDir` is sugar for `createWrapper: (i) => new LocalFileWrapper({path: tmpDir + '/stream-sorting-<pid>-<uuid>-' + i + '.jsonl'})`. Pass `createWrapper` directly for `MemoryWrapper` (tests), S3, sharded volumes, etc. `LocalFileWrapper` has no default `tmpDir` because Linux `/tmp` is commonly tmpfs — pass the path explicitly.
- `batchSize` — soft cap on in-memory items per run. Default `10000`. Tune up for compact items (more items fit in RAM → fewer disk writes); tune down for fat items.
- `stable` — default `true`. When `true`, ties (`compare` returns 0) are broken by input order via an internal monotonic sequence tag added to each item and stripped before emission. Set `false` if your comparator already encodes a tiebreaker (e.g., sorting by `(price, id)`) — saves ~8 bytes per item on disk plus one extra comparison per merge step.
- `onProgress(stats)` — called on natural event boundaries (run-complete during pre-sort, merge-start). Stats shape: `{phase: 'pre-sort' | 'final-merge', itemsRead, itemsWritten, runsCreated}`.
- `keepTempFiles` — default `false`. When `true`, skips wrapper deletion after the algorithm completes (file handles released via `close()`, but underlying storage preserved for debugging or re-merge).

**Returns:** an async generator. Iterate via `for await`, or convert at the boundary:

```js
for await (const item of sort(input, opts)) ...                     // direct
readableFrom(sort(input, opts)).pipe(downstream)                    // Node Readable
ReadableStream.from(sort(input, opts)).pipeTo(webDst)               // Web ReadableStream
```

**Run formation.** Pulls items into an in-memory buffer up to `batchSize`; when the buffer is full and another item arrives, sorts the buffer with `Array.prototype.sort` and drains it to a fresh wrapper via `consume()`. The last batch is held until input is exhausted.

**In-memory fast path.** When `input.length ≤ batchSize`, no wrapper is created — the algorithm sorts the buffer in memory and yields directly.

**Single-run path.** When the algorithm flushes exactly one run, it skips the merge and streams the run back directly via `wrapper.openReader()`.

**K-way merge.** When two or more runs exist, the algorithm wraps each `wrapper.openReader()` (`AsyncIterable<T>`) via `stream-chain`'s `readableFrom` to a Node Readable, then composes `stream-join`'s `mergeSorted(readables, lessFn)` for the final merge. The output of the merge is iterated via `for await` and yielded as our generator's output. (The internal Node-Readable wrap is an implementation detail because stream-join 2.x takes `Readable[]`; an open queue item tracks moving stream-join to AsyncIterable-based APIs in a 3.0.)

**Stability mechanism.** Each item gets a `{item, tag}` envelope during the pull phase (`tag` is a monotonic counter); the internal comparator compares `.item` first, ties broken by `.tag`. Envelopes are stripped on emit.

**Cleanup.** A `finally` block runs `wrapper.delete()` on every wrapper created (or `wrapper.close()` if `keepTempFiles: true`). Comparator throws, input errors, and consumer breaks all trigger cleanup.

**Edge cases:**
- Empty input: emits zero values and returns.
- Input fits in one batch: in-memory fast path (no disk, no wrapper).
- Input emits exactly one full run: single-run path (wrapper used, no merge).
- Comparator throws during sort or merge: error propagates to the consumer; cleanup runs.
- Input stream errors: error propagates; cleanup runs.

### `polyphaseSort(input, options)` — polyphase merge sort (shipped)

Fixed-file-budget companion to `sort`. Uses exactly `K` files regardless of input size — for bounded file budgets, or storage spread across drives / buckets / machines (one wrapper per backend). Same in/out contract as `sort`: `input` is `AsyncIterable<T> | Iterable<T>`, returns an `AsyncIterable<T>`.

**Signature:**

```ts
function polyphaseSort<T>(
  input: AsyncIterable<T> | Iterable<T>,
  options:
    | {compare: (a: T, b: T) => number}
    | {lessFn: (a: T, b: T) => boolean}
    & (
        | {files: ObjectStreamWrapper<unknown>[]}
        | {k?: number; tmpDir: string}
        | {k?: number; createWrapper: (fileIndex: number) => ObjectStreamWrapper<unknown>}
      )
    & {
        batchSize?: number;       // default 10000
        stable?: boolean;          // default true
        onProgress?: (stats: PolyphaseSortProgressStats) => void;
        keepTempFiles?: boolean;   // default false
      }
): AsyncGenerator<T, void, void>;
```

**Parameters:** `compare` / `lessFn`, `batchSize`, `stable`, `keepTempFiles` behave exactly as in `sort`. Storage is one of:

- `files` — explicit wrappers, one per file. `K = files.length` (minimum 3). User-owned: `close()`d at the end, not deleted.
- `k` (default 4, minimum 3) with `tmpDir` — `k` built-in `LocalFileWrapper`s under `tmpDir` (no default — tmpfs footgun).
- `k` with `createWrapper: (fileIndex) => ObjectStreamWrapper` — factory for the `k` wrappers.

`onProgress(stats)` reports `{phase: 'pre-sort' | 'merge' | 'final-merge', itemsRead, itemsWritten, passesComplete, virtualSeries, files: [{role, runsRemaining}]}`.

**Distribution.** Pre-sorts input into runs and writes them across the `K − 1` input files toward a perfect generalized-Fibonacci distribution; the shortfall (when the real run count is not perfect) is tracked as virtual (empty) runs.

**Merge phases.** Repeatedly merges the `K − 1` inputs into the one output file via a hand-written series-aware merge — a run ends at a sort-order break (`lessFn`). When an input drains it becomes the next output and the old output rejoins the inputs. Run counts are kept arithmetically (clean Fibonacci); accidentally adjacent in-order runs simply read back as one longer run, and EOF corrects the bookkeeping. The final merge (every file down to ≤ 1 run) streams straight to the caller. In-memory fast path like `sort` when `input ≤ batchSize`.

**Stability.** Same `{item, tag}` envelope as `sort` — essential here because items are reshuffled across passes. The merge is hand-written, not `stream-join`'s `mergeSorted`.

**Why polyphase vs k-way.** Prefer `sort` on modern SSDs (single-pass merge, cheap file handles). Prefer `polyphaseSort` when the number of open files must be bounded, or storage is spread across expensive / remote backends.

### `join(inputs, options)` / `leftJoin` / `fullJoin` — key-based join of sorted streams

```ts
interface JoinInput<T, K> {
  input: AsyncIterable<T> | Iterable<T>;
  key?: (item: T) => K; // default: identity
  optional?: boolean; // default: false — when true, null-filled if absent at a key
}

function join<I extends Record<string, JoinInput<any, any>>, R>(
  inputs: I, // named map: { left: {input, key}, right: {input, key}, ... }
  options?: {
    compareKey?: (a: any, b: any) => number; // default: natural order
    lessKey?: (a: any, b: any) => boolean; // provide this OR compareKey
    combine?: (bag: Record<string, any | null>) => R | undefined; // default: bag => bag
    maxGroupSize?: number; // throw if an equal-key group exceeds this
  }
): AsyncGenerator<R, void, void>;
```

Import from `stream-sorting/sorted/join.js` (and `sorted/left-join.js`, `sorted/full-join.js`); all three are re-exported from the index.

**Pre-condition:** every input is sorted by its key under `compareKey`; an out-of-order input throws at runtime.

**Inputs are a named map.** Each descriptor's `key` extracts the join key (default identity); the map key names the input on input and in the result.

**Semantics:**
- **Inner by default** — a row emits only when every required input has the key.
- **Equal keys form a Cartesian product**, like SQL joins (`m × n` rows).
- **`combine` receives a named bag** keyed by the input names (`{left, right, …}`), absent optional inputs as `null`. Default returns the bag unchanged; returning `undefined` drops that combination (a join-time filter).
- **Outer joins via `optional`** — mark an input `optional: true` to null-fill it. `leftJoin` (first input required, rest optional) and `fullJoin` (all optional) are thin wrappers; for arbitrary requiredness across N inputs set `optional` per input on `join`.
- **N-way** — any number of inputs; composite/tuple keys need an explicit `compareKey`.

Implemented as a custom group-aware merge (the D3 exception, like `polyphaseSort`) sharing a peekable reader at `src/reader.js` — a flat `select` + `sortedInsert` merge can't express equal-key grouping plus the Cartesian product.

### `matching(primary, probe, options)` / `unmatched(...)` — key-based filters

```ts
interface FilterInput<T, K> {
  input: AsyncIterable<T> | Iterable<T>;
  key?: (item: T) => K; // default: identity
}
function matching<T>(
  primary: FilterInput<T, any>,
  probe: FilterInput<any, any>,
  options?: {compareKey?: (a: any, b: any) => number; lessKey?: (a: any, b: any) => boolean}
): AsyncGenerator<T, void, void>;
// `unmatched` has the same signature.
```

Import from `stream-sorting/sorted/matching.js` / `sorted/unmatched.js`. Emit rows of `primary` whose key is present (`matching`) or absent (`unmatched`) in `probe` — semi / anti-join filters. Whole rows pass through unchanged; no `combine`, no product, and **primary duplicates are preserved** (a filter, not a dedup); probe duplicates are ignored. Both inputs are `{input, key?}` descriptors sorted by key (`key` defaults to identity, so `probe` can be a bare key stream); `compareKey` / `lessKey`, default natural order. Closely related to keyed `intersection` / `difference`, but they keep the primary's whole rows. Throw on an out-of-order primary.

### `aggregate(master, children, options)` — group/fold sorted streams by key

```ts
type Fold<T, A, R> = {
  input: AsyncIterable<T> | Iterable<T>;
  key?: (item: T) => any;
  init?: () => A; // create a fresh accumulator (no args)
  fold?: (acc: A, item: T) => A; // default: push the item
  finalize?: (acc: A) => R; // default: identity
};

function aggregate<R>(
  master: (Fold<any, any, any> & {input: AsyncIterable<any> | Iterable<any>}) | ((key: any) => any),
  children: Record<string, Fold<any, any, any> & {required?: boolean}>,
  options?: {
    compareKey?: (a: any, b: any) => number;
    lessKey?: (a: any, b: any) => boolean;
    combine?: (base: any, parts: Record<string, any>) => R | undefined; // default {...base, ...parts}
    maxGroupSize?: number;
  }
): AsyncGenerator<R, void, void>;
```

Import from `stream-sorting/sorted/aggregate.js` (re-exported from the index). SQL-style `GROUP BY` over sorted streams: one output row per key, streaming and single-pass (only one group's accumulators are live; a scalar fold holds nothing).

**The master** drives the spine, in two forms:
- a **`{input, key, init?, fold?, finalize?}` descriptor** — an external master stream; its keys decide which rows emit (a master key with no children still emits; child items with no master are dropped). Duplicate master rows at a key fold into one base — **first row wins by default**; an `init`/`fold`/`finalize` can merge them.
- a **`key => object` function** — the base is synthesized from the group key (group-by); the spine is then the children's own distinct keys.

**Children** are a named map. Each folds its per-key group with `init()` (no args) / `fold(acc, item)` / `finalize(acc)`, scoped to the master's key boundaries — a master with no items for a child gets `finalize(init())` (e.g. `[]`, or `0` for a count). Default fold is collect-to-array. Every scalar SQL aggregate is a fold: COUNT, SUM, AVG (finalize divides), MIN/MAX, ARRAY_AGG (the default — ordering free since children arrive sorted), STRING_AGG, COUNT(DISTINCT) via a Set. `required: true` drops masters whose group for that child is empty.

**`combine(base, parts)`** builds each output row from the master base and the named bag of child results (default `{...base, ...parts}`; return `undefined` to drop the row). `compareKey` **or** `lessKey` orders keys (composite/tuple keys need an explicit comparator); `maxGroupSize` guards a runaway group.

**Multi-level nesting** (department → employee → equipment) is composition, not a built-in: a `join` to enrich foreign keys, a re-`sort` to the ancestor key path, then a flat `aggregate` per level (`aggregate` emits in key order, so its output feeds the next level still sorted). Implemented as the same custom group-aware merge sharing `src/reader.js`.

### `merge` / `union` / `intersection` / `difference` — value-based set ops

```ts
type SetOpOptions = {compare?: (a: any, b: any) => number; lessFn?: (a: any, b: any) => boolean};

function merge<T>(streams: Array<AsyncIterable<T> | Iterable<T>>, options?: SetOpOptions): AsyncGenerator<T, void, void>;
function union<T>(streams: Array<AsyncIterable<T> | Iterable<T>>, options?: SetOpOptions): AsyncGenerator<T, void, void>;
function intersection<T>(streams: Array<AsyncIterable<T> | Iterable<T>>, options?: SetOpOptions): AsyncGenerator<T, void, void>;
function difference<T>(streams: Array<AsyncIterable<T> | Iterable<T>>, options?: SetOpOptions): AsyncGenerator<T, void, void>;
```

Each takes an array of pre-sorted streams; the comparator defines both order and equality (default natural). Imported from `stream-sorting/sorted/{merge,union,intersection,difference}.js`.

- **`merge`** — k-way merge, **duplicates preserved** (was `mergeSorted`; the suite's foundational op, and what `union` builds on). Ties keep input order. Whether `stream-join` drops its `utils/merge-sorted` copy for this is still open (see `projects/stream-sorting/queue.md`).
- **`union`** — `merge` plus cross-stream (and within-stream) deduplication. `{1,2,3} ∪ {2,3,4} = {1,2,3,4}`.
- **`intersection`** — values present in **all** streams (≥ 2 inputs), deduped: advance the minimum head, emit once when every head agrees.
- **`difference`** — values in `streams[0]` not present in any of `streams[1..]`, deduped.

`union` / `intersection` / `difference` emit deduped sets; equality is "the comparator ranks neither below the other." An out-of-order input throws when the offending item is reached (best-effort where a stream's tail goes unconsumed).

### `sortJsonl(input, options)` — text-JSONL convenience over `sort`

```ts
function sortJsonl<T>(
  input: AsyncIterable<string | Uint8Array> | Iterable<string | Uint8Array>,
  options: SortOptions<T> & {
    parse?: (line: string) => unknown; // default JSON.parse
    stringify?: (item: unknown) => string; // default JSON.stringify
  }
): AsyncGenerator<string, void, void>;
```

Import from `stream-sorting/utils/sort-jsonl.js` (re-exported from the index). Parses a **text** JSONL stream into objects (via `stream-chain`'s `fixUtf8Stream` + `lines` — UTF-8-safe across chunk boundaries, tolerant of a missing final newline), runs `sort`, and re-emits JSONL text (`JSON.stringify(item) + '\n'` per item). Accepts every `sort` option (`compare`/`lessFn`, `tmpDir`/`createWrapper`, `batchSize`, `stable`, …) plus `parse` / `stringify`.

This is the **only** text-aware entry point — the rest of the package is object-mode in / object-mode out. `sortJsonl` is exactly the `stream-chain` composition (parse → `sort` → stringify) wrapped under a name; when sorting is one stage of a larger pipeline, compose `stream-chain` directly instead (JSONL framing is `stream-chain`'s job). Lives under `src/utils/` because it is sugar, not a new algorithm.

## Composition examples

### Sort a stream of records by ID

```js
import sort from 'stream-sorting/sort.js';
import {pipeline} from 'node:stream/promises';

await pipeline(
  input,
  sort(input, {compare: (a, b) => a.id - b.id, tmpDir: '/var/sort'}),
  output
);
```

### Join two large feeds by ID

```js
import sort from 'stream-sorting/sort.js';
import leftJoin from 'stream-sorting/sorted/left-join.js';
import readableFrom from 'stream-chain/utils/readableFrom.js';

const byId = (a, b) => a.id - b.id;

const sortedLeft = sort(left, {compare: byId, tmpDir: '/var/sort'});
const sortedRight = sort(right, {compare: byId, tmpDir: '/var/sort'});

const joined = leftJoin(
  {left: {input: sortedLeft, key: r => r.id}, right: {input: sortedRight, key: r => r.id}},
  {combine: ({left, right}) => ({...left, ...right})}
);

readableFrom(joined).pipe(output);
```

### Deduplicate across N pre-sorted feeds

```js
import union from 'stream-sorting/union.js';
const lessByKey = (a, b) => a.key < b.key;

union([feed1, feed2, feed3], lessByKey).pipe(output);
```

## Performance notes

- The `batchSize` knob is a **soft** cap — actual memory varies with item size. Tune for the workload.
- The k-way merge cost is `O(N log k)` where `N` is total items and `k` is the number of runs. Smaller `batchSize` → more runs → log factor grows; larger `batchSize` → fewer runs but higher peak RAM. Default is a starting point, not a prescription. `polyphaseSort` instead bounds the file count to `K` and pays more passes (~log_φ(R)).
- Disk I/O dominates for cardinalities that overflow RAM. SSDs are the assumed deployment target; spinning disks work but slower.
- The `serialize` / `deserialize` hooks are the per-item hot path on disk-backed runs; for high-throughput pipelines, custom binary encodings can outperform the default JSON.

## Composition with `stream-chain`

The package's outputs are plain `Readable` streams. They drop into `stream-chain` pipelines without adapters:

```js
import chain from 'stream-chain';
import sort from 'stream-sorting/sort.js';

const pipeline = chain([
  source,
  transform,
  sort(/* upstream */, {compare, tmpDir: '/var/sort'}),
  consumer
]);
```

## Composition with `stream-join`

`stream-sorting` builds on `stream-join`'s primitives but does not re-export them. If a user needs the lower-level merge tools directly:

```js
import select from 'stream-join/select.js';
import sortedInsert from 'stream-join/utils/sorted-insert.js';

// Hand-rolled k-way merge:
const merged = select(streams, {
  pick: items => 0,                      // smallest is always at index 0
  insert: sortedInsert((a, b) => a < b)
});
```

`stream-sorting`'s `merge` is the same composition wrapped under a friendlier name.
